podcast.body: Marcy Carsey and Tom Werner, executive producers of The Cosby Show, sought a no-frills family comedy in 1987, turning to Cosby writer Matt Williams to script a show about a blue-collar family. This was considered a radical idea given the opulence dominating TV with shows like Dallas, FalconCrust, The Cosby Show, and Empty Nest. Barr was signed for the lead role after appearing on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, where she was not nationally known. The show premiered on October 18, 1988, becoming an instant hit with 21.4 million households watching, making it the highest-rated debut of that season. It chronicled the tumultuous life of the working-class Conner family, featuring Barr's "brash, even caustic" character who often worried about money, yet thrived as a loving family. The series was regularly in the top three of the Nielsen ratings and remained in the top 20 until its final season. It hit its creative peak with provocative storylines such as DJ's masturbation obsession, Becky seeking birth control pills, Rosanne's PMS, and Darlene's first period. In its ninth and final season, the cash-strapped Conners won a $108 million Illinois State lottery prize, a moment critics and fans deemed "shark jumping." The series finale on May 20, 1997, revealed the entire ninth season was a fantasy of Barr's depressed blue-collar character; the Conners had not won the lottery, and Dan had died from a heart attack at the end of season 8. After the show finished, it lived on in syndication, drawing a new generation of viewers. "When the show went to air on October 18, 1988, the Connor family was an instant hit."

podcast.body: The series returned to television in March 2018, with its debut attracting 18.2 million viewers, making it the highest-rated comedy episode on any broadcast network in nearly four years. However, the show was canceled two months later after Barr posted a racist Twitter rant against Valerie Jarrett, a former adviser to President Barack Obama. "The debut of the new and improved Drozan had 18.2 million viewers, which made it the highest rated comedy episode on any broadcast network in nearly four years."
